title: Hooks — Automate Actions Around Claude's Work

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand what hooks are, know the three main hook types, and have a working hook that fires automatically when Claude Code modifies a file.

## What Are Hooks?

Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically at specific points in its workflow — before Claude uses a tool, after it uses a tool, or when it finishes a response.

Think of hooks as automation triggers: *"every time Claude edits a file, also do X."* You define X, and Claude Code handles the triggering.

Hooks are defined in `.claude/settings.json` under the `hooks` key. This file lives in your project root (not inside the `commands/` folder).

Common real-world uses:
- **Auto-lint:** Run `prettier --write` or `eslint --fix` on every file Claude edits, so your code is always formatted
- **Auto-test:** Run your test suite after Claude makes changes, so you see immediately if something broke
- **Logging:** Write a log entry every time Claude modifies a file, so you have an audit trail
- **Notifications:** Send a desktop notification or beep when Claude finishes a long task
- **Git auto-commit:** Automatically create a commit after every accepted change

## The Three Hook Types

**`PreToolUse`**
Runs *before* Claude uses a tool. Use cases: confirm you're in the right directory, check that a dependency is installed before Claude tries to use it, log what Claude is about to do.

**`PostToolUse`**
Runs *after* Claude uses a tool. This is the most commonly used hook. Use cases: lint the file that was just edited, run tests after a code change, log what was modified.

**`Stop`**
Runs when Claude finishes generating a complete response and is waiting for your input. Use cases: play a sound to signal Claude is done, send a notification.

Each hook type takes a list of matchers. The `matcher` field is a regex pattern that matches tool names — so you can trigger a hook only on `Write` calls, only on `Bash` calls, or any combination.

**Matcher syntax:** The `matcher` field uses regular expressions. Common patterns:
- `"Write"` — fires only on Write tool calls (creating or overwriting files)
- `"Edit"` — fires only on Edit tool calls (in-place edits)
- `"Write|Edit"` — fires on either
- `"Bash"` — fires when Claude runs a shell command
- `".*"` — fires on every tool use (broad — use carefully)

## A Real-World Hooks Example

Here's a `settings.json` with three useful hooks for a web development project:

- A PostToolUse hook that logs which file was modified
- A Stop hook that prints a "Claude is done" message
- A PreToolUse hook that echoes a warning before any Bash command runs

**Hooks run with your user permissions.** A hook that runs `rm -rf` would actually delete files. Keep hooks simple and deterministic. If you're adding a hook that runs a linter or formatter, make sure that tool is installed and working before you wire it up — a failing hook will interrupt Claude's workflow.

sections.title: Set Up a File-Edit Hook
sections.content:
Add a PostToolUse hook that prints a message in the terminal every time Claude modifies a file. Verify it fires.

**Step 1 — Create or open `.claude/settings.json`:**
In VS Code Explorer, look for `.claude/settings.json` in your project root. If it doesn't exist, create it. (The `.claude/` folder should already exist from lesson 7-7 when you created the `commands/` subfolder.)

**Step 2 — Add the hook:**
Paste this content into `.claude/settings.json`:
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "echo Claude just edited a file"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
Save the file.

**Step 3 — Launch Claude Code:**
```
cd Documents\ai-course-projects
claude
```

**Step 4 — Trigger the hook:**
Ask Claude to make a small change to any file:
```
Add an HTML comment at the top of exercises/about-me.html that says
"Last updated by Claude Code"
```
Review the diff and accept it.

**Step 5 — Observe the hook output:**
After Claude applies the change, you should see:
```
Claude just edited a file
```
Printed in your terminal. That's your hook firing.

**Step 6 — Upgrade the hook (optional):**
Change the hook to something more informative. On Windows (PowerShell), update the command to:
```
echo File modified at %TIME%
```
This prints the time of each edit, giving you a lightweight audit log.

**Real-world extension:** If you have Prettier installed (`npm install -g prettier`), replace the echo command with:
```
prettier --write %CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT_PATH%
```
This auto-formats every file Claude touches. That single hook line eliminates an entire class of manual formatting work.

**You've completed lesson 7-8.** You've configured a working hook and understand the three hook types. Hooks are one of Claude Code's most powerful features for building reliable, repeatable workflows. Next: the memory system.
